learn.intro: The years around 1400–1600 are often called the "Age of Exploration". But long before Columbus sailed in 1492, travellers like Ibn Battuta and Zheng He crossed huge distances, and great trade networks already linked Africa, Asia and Europe. Was there really an "Age of Exploration"?

blocks.p: Ibn Battuta, a scholar from Morocco (1304–c.1368), travelled roughly 120,000 km across North and West Africa, the Middle East, India and China, further than most European explorers who came after him. His travel account is known as the Rihla.

Zheng He, an admiral of Ming China (1371–1433), commanded seven huge naval expeditions between 1405 and 1433 across the Indian Ocean to Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa. His largest "treasure ships" were far bigger than anything Europe built for another century.
China chose to end these voyages in the 1430s for political and economic reasons, not because it lacked the ability to continue.
So by 1492, long-distance travel was well established, just not by Europeans and not across the Atlantic.

sections.title: 2. A world already connected

blocks.p: Four great networks linked much of Africa and Eurasia before 1492:

ul: The Silk Roads: overland and sea routes between China, Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe.
The Indian Ocean trade world: East Africa, Arabia, India, Southeast Asia and China, sailing with the predictable monsoon winds.
Trans-Saharan routes: West Africa to North Africa, trading especially gold and salt.
Arabian and Red Sea routes linking these systems together.

blocks.p: West African empires (Ghana, then Mali, then Songhay) grew rich on trans-Saharan trade. Mansa Musa of Mali's 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca was so lavish that it disrupted gold prices in Cairo.

Port cities such as Kilwa (East Africa), Calicut (India), Malacca (Southeast Asia) and Hormuz (Persian Gulf) were busy, cosmopolitan hubs. Arab, Persian, Gujarati and Chinese merchants dominated Indian Ocean trade for centuries before Vasco da Gama arrived in 1498.

evidence: Kilwa, Calicut, Malacca and Hormuz were major ports.

sections.title: 3. Is "Age of Exploration" a fair name?

blocks.p: Periodisation means how historians divide the past into named ages. "Age of Exploration" names the period after Europeans began travelling further, treating earlier non-European voyages as background. That is a Eurocentric framing: it sees world history mainly from Europe's point of view.

The label is not useless: European Atlantic and Indian Ocean voyages after 1492 did change the world dramatically. But "discovery" language is contested, because places Europeans "discovered" were usually already known to, and lived in by, other peoples. In this unit we use "encounter" or "arrival" more often than "discovery".

evidence: Europeans connected an already connected Afro-Eurasian world to the Americas.

sources.title: Ibn Battuta's Rihla (travel account)
sources.origin: Ibn Battuta's memories, written down by the scholar Ibn Juzayy in Morocco.
sources.purpose: To record his journeys for the ruler of Morocco and readers.
sources.usefulness: Rich detail on many societies. Written from memory years later and partly shaped by its writer, so details need checking.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: "Age of Exploration" is a fair name for the period 1400–1600. How far do you agree?
questions.asks: Weigh the case for the label (European voyages changed the world) against the case against (earlier non-European travel; Eurocentric).
steps: Give the case for the label with evidence (e.g. 1492).
Give the case against with precise evidence (Ibn Battuta, Zheng He).
questions.plan: 2 minutes planning, 9 minutes writing, 1 minute checking.

model.t: The label is only partly fair, because it treats European voyages as the start of exploration.
Zheng He led seven expeditions across the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433, decades before Columbus sailed in 1492.
This means long-distance exploration was already well established, so the label centres Europe rather than the whole world.
Therefore "Age of Exploration" describes Europe's experience better than the world's.

full: P: The label is fair / unfair to a large / some extent because…
some: P: qualified claim (highly / partly / to some extent…)
E: precise evidence (name, date, number, source)
E: explain with a connective (because / this meant that / therefore)
J: judgement that answers the question
